title: Macerata to the Potala: the Self-Taught Philologist, Eight Expeditions, and the Institute That Outlived the Regime
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Macerata and Rome: the Self-Taught Philologist

stops.name: Macerata, the birth in the Marche
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Giuseppe Tucci is born on the fifth of June 1894 at Macerata, a walled hill town in the Marche that had already given the Jesuit Matteo Ricci to China three hundred and forty-two years earlier. He teaches himself Hebrew, Chinese and Sanskrit before any university will admit him, working from grammars ordered by post into a house with no orientalist in it. At seventeen he publishes a set of Latin inscriptions in a German philological journal, which is how the professors in Rome first come across his name.
suggested_refs: The birth register of Macerata, 5 June 1894
The Casa di Matteo Ricci, in the same town, three centuries earlier
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

stops.name: Macerata, the Liceo Leopardi
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the 1907 enrolment year is attested (it.wikipedia), the month is conventional
stops.campa: He enters the Liceo Classico Giacomo Leopardi, a few streets from the house where he was born, and takes his diploma there on the twenty-fifth of June 1912. The curriculum is Latin and Greek; the languages he actually wants are kept for the evenings. Both Italian Wikipedia and Treccani place this school in Macerata. An earlier compilation moved it fifty-five kilometres south to Ascoli Piceno, where a different school will employ him later; the error is corrected here rather than carried forward.
suggested_refs: Liceo Classico Giacomo Leopardi, Macerata, diploma of 25 June 1912
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

stops.name: Rome, enrolment in classical philology
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In March 1913 Tucci enrols in classical philology at the University of Rome. The war takes him out of the lecture halls before he can finish, and the degree waits out the Isonzo. Through the interruption he keeps reading alone, on texts nobody has set him. The thesis he eventually writes has nothing to do with Cicero or Pindar. Its subject is the history of studies in oriental philosophy, which the faculty barely recognises as a field and certainly does not staff.
suggested_refs: The Faculty of Letters and Philosophy, University of Rome, matriculation register 1913
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

stops.name: Rome, the laurea after the war
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twelfth of July 1919 Tucci takes his doctorate with highest honours. He is twenty-five, and the war years sit inside the transcript as a gap nobody comments on. Rome has no chair in what he does. Italy in 1919 has no Tibetology and no faculty of Asian religion. What it has is a young man with Sanskrit, Chinese, Hebrew, Latin and Greek, and a diploma in the history of a discipline whose Italian version he will spend the next sixty years building.
suggested_refs: Doctoral thesis on the history of studies in oriental philosophy, University of Rome, 1919
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

stops.name: Ascoli Piceno, the Liceo-Ginnasio Stabili
stops.date_confidence: contested: Treccani gives 1920 and 'a few months', it.wikipedia gives 1919-1921
stops.campa: Tucci teaches for a stretch at the Liceo-Ginnasio Stabili in Ascoli Piceno, a provincial classroom of boys construing Virgil, the ordinary first employment of a brilliant classicist with nowhere better to go. Treccani calls the post a matter of months in 1920; Italian Wikipedia stretches it across 1919 to 1921, and the two are not reconciled. He marries Rosa Di Benedetto in the same period. The arrangement does not hold him: within a year he is back in Rome with a state appointment and a journal of his own to found.
suggested_refs: Liceo-Ginnasio Stabili, Ascoli Piceno, staff records 1919-1921
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

stops.name: Rome, the library of the Chamber of Deputies
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In January 1921 Tucci is made secretary of the library of the Chamber of Deputies, a salaried post among parliamentary papers that leaves his evenings free. In the same year he founds the journal Alle fonti delle religioni. It runs four years and is then absorbed, in 1925, into Raffaele Pettazzoni's Studi e materiali di Storia delle religioni; he is not a founder of Pettazzoni's review, though later summaries keep making him one. He holds the library post through the decade, including the years he spends in India.
suggested_refs: Biblioteca della Camera dei deputati, Rome, staff appointment of January 1921
Alle fonti delle religioni, 1921-1925
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'
Wikipedia (it), 'Studi e materiali di storia delle religioni'

stops.name: Rome, the libera docenza
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Storia della filosofia cinese antica appears in 1922, the first history of early Chinese philosophy written in Italian. In 1923 he obtains the libera docenza in Far Eastern languages and literatures, and his son is born and named Ananda, for the Buddha's companion. By 1924 he is teaching Indian and Far Eastern religions and philosophies at the University of Rome. The credential is a licence to lecture. There is still no chair in the subject anywhere in Italy, and in November 1925 he sails for India.
suggested_refs: Giuseppe Tucci, Storia della filosofia cinese antica (1922)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

segments.name: Five and a Half Years in Asia

stops.name: Santiniketan, the university in the mango grove
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the November 1925 departure with Carlo Formichi is attested, the arrival month is not
stops.campa: Tucci sails for India in November 1925 with Carlo Formichi and stays five and a half years. At Santiniketan he joins the university Rabindranath Tagore built in a mango grove, where classes are held under trees and the disciplines are not walled off from one another. He teaches Italian and Chinese and studies Buddhism, Tibetan and Bengali, which is the exchange he came for. The philologist who learned Sanskrit from grammars in Macerata now hears it argued aloud by men who never stopped using it.
suggested_refs: Visva-Bharati University, Santiniketan, founded by Rabindranath Tagore
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

stops.name: Dhaka, the university lectures
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the post is attested, the year assigned within the 1925-1930 circuit is not
stops.campa: Tucci lectures at the University of Dhaka in eastern Bengal, one station in a circuit that also takes him to Benares and Calcutta. He is a European teaching Chinese and Italian to Indian students while taking Tibetan lessons from them in return, an arrangement no Roman faculty of the period would have recognised as scholarship. By 1930 he has a working command of the languages of the Himalayan frontier, acquired inside the subcontinent rather than out of European libraries.
suggested_refs: University of Dhaka, Italian and Chinese teaching, later 1920s

stops.name: Benares, reading with the pandits
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the Benares teaching is attested, the year within the circuit is not
stops.campa: At Benares, on the Ganges, Tucci works among pandits in the oldest continuous school of Sanskrit learning in the world. He reads with men whose training is oral and genealogical, teacher to pupil across centuries, and he takes their method as seriously as their manuscripts. Later, in Tibetan monasteries, he will look for the same two things together: the book on the shelf, and the person who can still explain what is in it. The Sanskrit he brings out of Benares is the language he will read the Tibetan canon against.
suggested_refs: Banaras Hindu University and the Sanskrit pandit schools of Varanasi

stops.name: Calcutta, the meeting at Dasgupta's house
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year
stops.campa: Tucci teaches at Calcutta University, and in 1929, at the house of the philosopher Surendranath Dasgupta, he meets a young Romanian student of Sanskrit named Mircea Eliade, who will fold this city into a mythology of his own. Calcutta is Swami Vivekananda's birthplace and burial ground and the rail head from which every European bound for Sikkim and the Tibetan frontier departs. Two men who will spend their lives explaining Asia to Europe sit in one room, both of them still at the beginning of it.
suggested_refs: The house of Surendranath Dasgupta, Calcutta, 1929

stops.name: Kashmir, the corridor to the plateau
stops.date_confidence: inferred: it.wikipedia places the Kashmir travel in the later 1920s without a month
stops.campa: Tucci moves through Kashmir in the later 1920s, the corridor of passes and river valleys that links British India to Ladakh and the plateau beyond. Helena Blavatsky claimed to have crossed here into Little Tibet in 1856, guided by a Tartar shaman, and Savitri Devi will climb to the Amarnath cave in 1936. Tucci comes with survey equipment, a camera and letters of introduction. The route is the same route; what differs is that he intends to come back with plates and inscriptions rather than with revelations.
suggested_refs: The Kashmir-Ladakh caravan corridor into the Tibetan borderlands

stops.name: Darjeeling, where Europe stops
stops.date_confidence: attested for February-March 1930
stops.campa: In February 1930 Tucci travels to Darjeeling, the hill station where Europe stops and the Tibetan frontier begins. Hermann Keyserling had come this way in 1912 and written the mountains up as a philosopher's vision. Tucci comes to hire porters. The town holds the transport agents, the Tibetan-speaking clerks and the permits without which no caravan moves north. Every expedition he mounts over the next eighteen years is assembled in a town like this one, and none of the work he is famous for happens anywhere a road reaches.
suggested_refs: Darjeeling as staging town for Himalayan expeditions, 1900-1950

stops.name: Leh, the summer in Ladakh
stops.date_confidence: attested for June-September 1930
stops.campa: Tucci spends the summer of 1930 at Leh, his second visit to Ladakh, working through the monasteries strung along the upper Indus. Ladakh is Tibetan in language, script, architecture and rite, and it lies inside British India, which means a scholar may work there without a permit from Lhasa. He photographs, copies inscriptions and buys manuscripts. The Tibetan world he documents at Leh lies wholly outside Tibet's political border, and he plans every later expedition on that geography rather than on the map of states.
suggested_refs: The Buddhist monasteries of the upper Indus around Leh

segments.name: Naples, and the Founding of IsMEO

stops.name: Naples, the first Italian chair of Chinese
stops.date_confidence: contested: Treccani dates the appointment 1930, en.wikipedia dates the return and the chair 1931
stops.campa: Tucci comes back to Italy and is called to the chair of Chinese language and literature at the Oriental Institute of Naples, the first such chair in the country. Treccani puts the appointment in 1930; English Wikipedia puts his return and the chair in 1931, and the two are left standing against each other here. The post gives him a salary, a title and the standing to ask ministries for expedition money. From Naples he begins planning the campaigns into western Tibet that will fill the decade.
suggested_refs: The chair of Chinese language and literature, Istituto Orientale di Napoli
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

stops.name: Gangtok, the third expedition sets out
stops.date_confidence: attested for July 1931; the numbering of the expedition is contested
stops.campa: In July 1931 Tucci sets out through Gangtok, the Chogyal's capital in Sikkim, on what Italian Wikipedia counts as the third expedition of his career and the first of the great western Tibet campaigns. Sikkim is the antechamber: the last country where a European travels on British paper before crossing into one that issues its own. The Italian sources list the major expeditions as 1931, 1933, 1935, 1937 and 1939; English Wikipedia groups the western Tibet trips as 1931, 1933 and 1935. Neither count is adopted over the other.
suggested_refs: Gangtok and the Sikkim route to the Tibetan frontier

stops.name: Kathmandu, the stupa above the valley
stops.date_confidence: attested for November 1931, one of four pre-war Nepal visits
stops.campa: Tucci reaches the Kathmandu valley in November 1931, one of four visits he makes before the war. He climbs to Swayambhunath above the valley floor, the hilltop stupa with painted eyes on four sides, and works through the Newar Buddhist shrines and the manuscript libraries that have preserved Sanskrit texts lost in India itself. Nepal is at this date almost closed to foreigners. What he can photograph he photographs, and what he cannot photograph he copies out by hand.
stops.quote: Then, in five journeys in Nepal it appeared to me that the history of this country is not contained within the limits of the valley where Kathmandu, Patan or Bhatgaon are located.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Tucci, Preliminary Report on Two Scientific Expeditions in Nepal (Rome, IsMEO, 1956), Introduction, p. 1, written a quarter of a century later
suggested_refs: Swayambhunath and the Newar manuscript libraries of the Kathmandu valley
sources: Giuseppe Tucci, Preliminary Report on Two Scientific Expeditions in Nepal (1956), archive.org in.gov.ignca.6480

stops.name: Rome, IsMEO founded with Gentile
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the sixteenth of February 1933 the Italian Institute for the Middle and Far East is founded in Rome, Tucci and the philosopher Giovanni Gentile its founders and Tucci its managing vice-president. IsMEO is housed at Palazzo Brancaccio and funded by a fascist state that wants prestige in Asia. It will pay for everything Tucci does for the next fifty years: expeditions, excavations, a publication series, eventually a museum. Gentile will be shot by partisans in Florence in April 1944.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Brancaccio, via Merulana, seat of IsMEO from 1933
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

stops.name: Yatung, the Chumbi crossing
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: no consulted source names Tucci at Yatung; the route is inferred from period traffic
stops.campa: The caravans cross out of Sikkim into Tibetan territory through the Chumbi valley and the trade post at Yatung, the needle's eye between British India and the plateau. No consulted source places Tucci here by name; the crossing is reconstructed from the standard Sikkim to Tibet traffic of the period, which had no practical alternative. Beyond it the party moves on mules and yaks at the pace of the fifteenth century, carrying cameras, glass plates, notebooks and cash for the purchase of manuscripts.
suggested_refs: The Chumbi valley trade route between Sikkim and Tibet, 1900-1950
sources: Reconstruction from standard 1930s Sikkim-Tibet caravan geography

stops.name: Toling, the rain on the frescoes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1933 expedition; the month is inferred
stops.campa: Tucci reaches Toling in far western Tibet, the monastery founded by the kings of Guge, and finds the roof long unrepaired and rain coming through onto the wall paintings. He records the condition in his expedition report along with the judgement that the place is among the oldest and finest in Tibet. The warning is printed and goes unheeded. What his plates and drawings preserve of these frescoes becomes, after the destruction of the following decades, a substantial part of what is known about them.
stops.quote: the monastery of Toling is one of the oldest, richest and finest of Tibet
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Tucci, expedition report on western Tibet, quoted in Wikipedia (en), 'Toling Monastery'
suggested_refs: Tucci's photographic plates of the Toling wall paintings, 1933

stops.name: Tsaparang, the capital of Guge
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1933 and 1935 expeditions; the month is inferred
stops.campa: Above the Sutlej gorge stands Tsaparang, the cliff capital of the vanished kingdom of Guge, its palaces and temples cut into a ridge of eroded earth. Tucci works here on two expeditions, documenting the painted chapels of a Buddhist civilisation that ended in the seventeenth century. He is also buying and reading. Among the manuscripts he turns up in western Tibet are two Tibetan pilgrim itineraries of the Swat valley, and those two texts will send him, twenty years later, to Pakistan with a spade.
stops.quote: During my travels in western Tibet I was fortunate enough to find two texts which are a kind of itinerary of the Swat Valley.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Tucci, Travels of Tibetan Pilgrims in the Swat Valley (Calcutta, Greater India Society, 1940), Introduction, p. 2
suggested_refs: The ruined palace-temples of Tsaparang, documented in Indo-Tibetica
sources: Giuseppe Tucci, Travels of Tibetan Pilgrims in the Swat Valley (1940), archive.org full text

stops.name: Tashilhunpo, Shigatse
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1930s expeditions; the year and month here are inferred
stops.campa: At Shigatse, seat of the Panchen Lama, Tucci examines Tashilhunpo, one of the great Gelug foundations, and the libraries and murals that feed straight into the volumes of Indo-Tibetica. The monastery holds one of the largest manuscript collections on the plateau outside Lhasa itself, built up over four centuries of Gelug patronage and endowment. Tucci arrives with letters of introduction, an interpreter and a plate camera, and leaves with an inventory that will anchor years of publication back in Rome.
suggested_refs: Tashilhunpo Monastery, Shigatse, and its manuscript collections

stops.name: Sakya, the initiation
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1935; the month is inferred
stops.campa: At Sakya in 1935 the abbot Ngawang Thutob Wangdrag confers a Buddhist initiation on Tucci. He practises afterwards, and in later years describes himself as the reincarnation of a Tibetan lama. The scholar who came to catalogue is received as a disciple, and the two roles never afterwards separate cleanly in anything he writes about Tibet. The grey monastery of Sakya, with its Mongol-era library walled in behind the assembly hall, holds the largest surviving collection of its kind on the plateau.
suggested_refs: Sakya Monastery and its walled library of Mongol-era manuscripts

stops.name: Kailash, the mountain he does not circle
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the geography of the western Tibet routes; no source places Tucci on the pilgrimage circuit
stops.campa: The western Tibet itineraries pass within sight of Kailash, the mountain that Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and Bonpo all walk around, and Manasarovar, the high lake below it. No consulted source puts Tucci on the pilgrimage circuit; his documented attention stays fixed on the ruined monasteries of Guge. Miguel Serrano will reach these same coordinates in 1957 in search of a mountain he says is found within. Tucci passes the sacred peak on his way to a fresco with a hole in the roof above it.
suggested_refs: The Kailash-Manasarovar pilgrimage circuit, crossed by the Guge caravan routes
sources: Reconstruction from the geography of Tucci's 1933 and 1935 western Tibet routes

stops.name: Tokyo, sent as Mussolini's representative
stops.date_confidence: attested for November 1936 to January 1937; the April 1937 radio address is a separate later event
stops.campa: From November 1936 to January 1937 Tucci is in Japan as Mussolini's personal representative, attending the opening of the Italian-Japanese Institute in Tokyo. He gives a radio address there in April 1937 and later sits on the editorial board of the propaganda magazine Yamato. Speeches from the mission invoke racial purity. The scholarship and the politics run on one budget: IsMEO, which pays for the Tibetan expeditions, is an organ of the state that sends him to Tokyo.
suggested_refs: The Italian-Japanese Institute, Tokyo, opened during Tucci's 1936-1937 mission
The propaganda magazine Yamato and its editorial board

stops.name: Samye, the mandala on the ground
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed: the 1937 central Tibet expedition is attested, Tucci's presence at Samye is not
stops.campa: Tucci conducts a central Tibet expedition in 1937. Samye, the first Buddhist monastery built in Tibet, laid out as a mandala with a central temple and four continents ringed around it, stands among the ancient foundations his central Tibet work examines. No consulted source names him inside its walls in this year, and the stop is a reconstruction from his published interest in the architecture. The ground plan of Samye is the ground plan of the book on mandalas he will publish in 1949.
suggested_refs: Samye Monastery, founded under Trisong Detsen c.763-779 CE
Giuseppe Tucci, Theory and Practice of the Mandala (1949)
sources: Reconstruction from Tucci's published work on Tibetan sacred architecture

stops.name: Rome, the race question
stops.date_confidence: contested: the reports of race-commission service and of a signature are unresolved in the sources
stops.campa: In 1938 the regime publishes the Manifesto della Razza and Italy acquires racial laws. Tucci is reported to have sat on a race-studies commission and is sometimes said to have signed the manifesto, though no documentary evidence of a signature has ever been produced. The same body of scholarship credits him with helping the Jewish analyst Ernst Bernhard escape deportation. Italian Wikipedia records both claims and resolves neither, and they are left here exactly as found.
suggested_refs: The Manifesto della Razza, July 1938, and the dispute over its signatories
sources: Wikipedia (it), 'Giuseppe Tucci', citing divided scholarly opinion

stops.name: Rome, IsMEO falls silent
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1944; the month follows the Allied entry into Rome on 4 June
stops.campa: The Allies enter Rome in June 1944 and IsMEO's activities stop. The institute has spent eleven years as the cultural arm of a state that no longer exists, and Gentile, its co-founder, has been shot in Florence in April. Tucci's Asian collections sit in Palazzo Brancaccio with no budget and no government behind them. He has not seen Tibet since 1939 and will not see it again for four years. Nothing in the record suggests he expected the institute to outlive the regime that built it.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Brancaccio under Allied occupation, 1944

stops.name: Rome, the epuration
stops.date_confidence: attested for July 1944
stops.campa: In July 1944 Tucci is brought before the epuration commissions set up to strip fascist appointees out of Italian public life. The charge is his relationship with the regime: the Royal Academy membership of 1929, the Foreign Ministry assignment of 1927, the Tokyo mission, the institute a fascist government paid for. The proceedings hang over him for eighteen months. Treccani records them plainly. The commission's reasoning is not printed in any source reachable here.
suggested_refs: The Italian epuration commissions, 1944-1946, and Tucci's file
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

stops.name: Rome, cleared and restored
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the eighth of January 1946 Tucci is cleared and reinstated to his academic post. In 1947 he is made president of the reconstituted IsMEO, which he will hold until 1978 and then keep as honorary president until his death. The institution passes intact out of Mussolini's Italy into the republic, the same founder at its head and a new letterhead over the door. Within a year he is on the road to Lhasa at the head of the largest expedition of his life.
suggested_refs: The reconstituted IsMEO under the Italian Republic, from 1947
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

stops.name: Kalimpong, the caravan assembled
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from standard Tibet-expedition logistics; no source dates Tucci here
stops.campa: Kalimpong, the trade town at the head of the old mule road to Lhasa, is where a Tibet expedition is assembled: porters hired, permits collected, pack animals bought, loads weighed and weighed again. No consulted source names Tucci here by date, and the stop is reconstructed from the logistics every party of the period followed. He is fifty-four, the war is over, and the Tibetan government has issued a permit that within three years will be beyond the reach of any foreigner alive.
suggested_refs: Kalimpong and the mule road to Lhasa, assembly point for Tibet expeditions
sources: Reconstruction from standard Tibet-expedition logistics of the period

stops.name: Potala Palace, the audience
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1948; the month is inferred
stops.campa: On his eighth and final Tibetan expedition Tucci reaches Lhasa and is received at the Potala Palace by the fourteenth Dalai Lama, who is thirteen years old. Tenzing Norgay, five years short of Everest, travels with the party. Tucci arrives with a permit, a photographer and an audience appointment, at the very end of the era when a foreign scholar could still reach this city with paperwork rather than by stealth. Within little more than a decade the plateau he has spent twenty years cataloguing will be closed to him for good.
suggested_refs: The Potala Palace audience of 1948, with Tenzing Norgay in the party

stops.name: Drepung, the monastic town
stops.date_confidence: reconstructed from the standard 1948 Lhasa itinerary; no source names Tucci inside
stops.campa: Drepung, west of Lhasa, was once the largest monastery in the world, a walled town of whitewashed buildings holding thousands of monks. It falls inside the circuit any visitor of 1948 makes and inside Tucci's documented survey pattern, though no consulted source places him within its walls. He has spent twenty years reading the literature these colleges produced. The institution he is looking at has eleven years left before the rising of 1959 and the flight of the Dalai Lama empty it.
suggested_refs: Drepung Monastery before 1959
sources: Reconstruction from the standard itinerary of Western visitors to Lhasa in 1948

stops.name: Rome, Tibetan Painted Scrolls
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year; the volume count is contested
stops.campa: Tibetan Painted Scrolls appears in Rome in 1949, the study of thangka painting that establishes Tibetan art history as a subject, together with Theory and Practice of the Mandala. English Wikipedia describes the Painted Scrolls in three volumes and Treccani in two, and the discrepancy is left standing. The material is the harvest of eight expeditions, and it comes out in the year the People's Liberation Army completes its conquest of China and turns toward the plateau.
suggested_refs: Giuseppe Tucci, Tibetan Painted Scrolls (Rome, 1949)
Giuseppe Tucci, Theory and Practice of the Mandala (1949)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

segments.name: Nepal, Swat, and the Archaeological Turn

stops.name: Kathmandu valley, the first formal expedition
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1952; the month is not given in the sources
stops.campa: Tucci returns to Nepal in 1952 on a formally organised IsMEO expedition, the improvised itineraries of his younger years replaced by an institutional mandate, and comes back again in 1954. Tibet is closing behind him. The Chinese entry of 1950 and the agreement of 1951 end foreign fieldwork on the plateau, and Nepal, newly opened after the fall of the Rana regime, becomes the one place where a Tibetologist can still work inside a living Tibetan-speaking world.
stops.quote: During my Tibetan travels I realized the importance of a better knowledge of the cultural and political history of Nepal for the investigation of the evolution of Tibetan culture.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Tucci, Preliminary Report on Two Scientific Expeditions in Nepal (Rome, IsMEO, 1956), Introduction, p. 1
suggested_refs: Giuseppe Tucci, Preliminary Report on Two Scientific Expeditions in Nepal (Rome, IsMEO, 1956)
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

stops.name: Tukucha, the temple of the queen
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1954 expedition; the month is not given
stops.campa: North of the Annapurna massif, on the salt road up the Kali Gandaki gorge, Tucci works at Tukucha among the Thakali. He describes three small temples, the oldest called the temple of the queen, and paintings he will not date closer than the sixteenth century. He records the hearth cult too, the fire in the middle of the kitchen inside its low earth wall, reprinting his own 1953 travel diary Tra Giungle e Pagode to say it. The 1956 report gives the kitchen fire as much space as the inscriptions.
stops.quote: These paintings are important, for, so far as I know, they are the only example of local art uninfected by Nepalese influences.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Tucci, Preliminary Report on Two Scientific Expeditions in Nepal (Rome, IsMEO, 1956), p. 10, on the temple of the queen at Tukucha
suggested_refs: The three temples of Tukucha and the Thakali hearth cult, described in the 1956 report
sources: Giuseppe Tucci, Preliminary Report on Two Scientific Expeditions in Nepal (1956), archive.org in.gov.ignca.6480
Giuseppe Tucci, Tra Giungle e Pagode (1953), quoted in the same report

stops.name: Swat, the reconnaissance at Butkara
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1955 reconnaissance; excavation from 1956 under Domenico Faccenna
stops.campa: Under the patronage of the Wali of Swat, Miangul Jahan Zeb, Tucci opens Italian archaeology in Pakistan in 1955 with a reconnaissance of the Swat valley. The Tibetan pilgrim itineraries he found in western Tibet twenty years earlier had already told him where Uddiyana was. Excavation at the Butkara stupa begins in 1956 under Domenico Faccenna, who directs the field work while Tucci directs the mission. The Gandharan sequence that comes out of the trench runs back to the third century before Christ.
stops.quote: It is now accepted by all scholars that Uddiyana must be located in the Swat Valley.
stops.quote_source: Giuseppe Tucci, Travels of Tibetan Pilgrims in the Swat Valley, Greater India Studies No. 2 (Calcutta, Greater India Society, 1940), Introduction, p. 1, opening sentence
suggested_refs: Butkara I, excavated 1956-1962 under Domenico Faccenna for IsMEO
sources: Treccani, Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, 'Tucci, Giuseppe'

stops.name: Ghazni, the Ghaznavid capital
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1956 as the start of the Ghazni work
stops.campa: IsMEO's archaeology reaches Ghazni in Afghanistan from 1956, into the ruins of the Ghaznavid capital that ruled from Persia to the Punjab in the eleventh century. Tucci is sixty-two and no longer primarily a Tibetologist. He runs a network of missions across a belt of Asia between the Indus and the Iranian plateau. The institute he founded in 1933 to give a fascist government prestige in Asia is now digging in Pakistan and Afghanistan on a republic's budget.

stops.name: Rome, the museum proposed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year
stops.campa: In 1957 Tucci proposes the founding of a national museum of oriental art in Rome, to hold what the expeditions and the excavations have been shipping home for a quarter of a century. It opens at Palazzo Brancaccio in the Esquilino, in the same building as his institute. In the same year he publishes Storia della filosofia indiana. The collection is the physical residue of a career: Tibetan paintings, Gandharan sculpture, Nepalese bronzes and the Swat material, gathered under one roof.

stops.name: Persepolis, the Iranian involvement
stops.date_confidence: contested in substance: the Iranian work 1959-1978 is attested, the Persepolis attribution is not
stops.campa: From 1959 until 1978 Tucci directs Italian archaeological work in Iran. Italian Wikipedia supports that and nothing narrower. The excavation itself was in Sistan, at Shahr-i Sokhta; IsMEO's presence at Persepolis was a restoration mission conducted by Giuseppe and Ann Britt Tilia, and the standard accounts of the Achaemenid site credit its excavation to Herzfeld, Schmidt and Godard. An earlier compilation placed Tucci at Persepolis. The coordinate is kept and the claim is corrected.

stops.name: Rome, the chair laid down
stops.date_confidence: contested: Treccani gives retirement 1969, it.wikipedia 1968; both give emeritus 1970
stops.campa: Tucci gives up his Roman chair at seventy-four or seventy-five. Treccani puts the retirement in 1969, Italian Wikipedia in 1968, and both agree he is made emeritus in 1970. The claim repeated in the research pool, that he taught at La Sapienza until his death, is wrong by fourteen years. He goes on directing IsMEO, publishing and travelling. What ends here is the lecturing, the last of the ordinary academic obligations he had spent forty years arranging his expeditions around.

stops.name: New Delhi, the Nehru Award
stops.date_confidence: resolved to 1976: en.wikipedia's own award list gives 1976 for Tucci and 1978 for Nichidatsu Fujii, against the 1978 in its Tucci article
stops.campa: India gives Tucci the Jawaharlal Nehru Award for International Understanding. English Wikipedia's article on him dates the award 1978; English Wikipedia's own list of the prize gives 1976 for Tucci and 1978 for Nichidatsu Fujii, and Treccani gives 1976. The contradiction is one-sided rather than a real dispute, and it is resolved here to 1976. Fifty years after he sailed for Santiniketan to teach Italian in Tagore's mango grove, the country he learned his Asia in names him for it.

stops.name: San Polo dei Cavalieri, the death
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinates reconcile three conflicting figures in the research pool to it.wikipedia's
stops.campa: Giuseppe Tucci dies at San Polo dei Cavalieri, in the hills east of Rome, on the fifth of April 1984, aged eighty-nine. He had shared the Balzan Prize for History with Ernest Labrousse in 1979, and married a third time, Francesca Bonardi, in 1971. The bibliography left behind him runs past three hundred and sixty books and articles in six languages. No source consulted states where he is buried, or in what form, or who attended. The tomb is a gap in this record and it is left standing as one.

stops.name: Rome, Largo Giuseppe Tucci
stops.date_confidence: attested for the date; the coordinates are the generic Rome centroid, no better figure reachable
stops.campa: Rome inaugurates Largo Giuseppe Tucci on the twenty-fifth of May 2010 and the naming is protested. Italian Wikipedia records objections from the city's Jewish community and from parliamentarians, on the ground of his alleged support for the Manifesto della Razza. The square keeps the name. The charge brought against it in 2010 is the charge the epuration commission heard in July 1944, and the outcome is the one that commission reached in January 1946.

stops.name: EUR, the collections moved
stops.date_confidence: attested for 2016; the month is not given
stops.campa: The museum built on Tucci's collections and formally named for him in 2005 is absorbed in 2016 into the Museo delle Civiltà and moved out to the Palazzo delle Scienze in EUR, the district Mussolini raised for a world's fair the war cancelled. His library of some twenty-five thousand volumes had already gone, after IsIAO's liquidation in 2012, to the Biblioteca Nazionale. Sources consulted do not say whether the Tibetan photographs and manuscripts followed the art or stayed with the books.
